==Problem==
Let <imath>f(n)=n^3-5n^2+2n+8</imath> and <imath>g(n)=n^3-6n^2+5n+12.</imath> What is the sum of all integers <imath>n</imath> such that <imath>\tfrac{f(n)}{g(n)}</imath> is an integer?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}~2\qquad\textbf{(B)}~3\qquad\textbf{(C)}~4\qquad\textbf{(D)}~5\qquad\textbf{(E)}~6</imath>

== Solution 1 ==
Observe that both <imath>f(n)</imath> and <imath>g(n)</imath> can be factored using the [[rational root theorem]]. By trying out a few values, we get that <imath>n = -1</imath> is a root of <imath>f(n)</imath>. Then, we can use synthetic division (regular polynomial division works, too) to get the other roots of <imath>f(n)</imath>, which are <imath>n = 4</imath> and <imath>n = 2</imath>. Now we factor <imath>g(n)</imath>. By inspection, <imath>n = -1</imath> also works on <imath>g(n)</imath>, and so synthetic division and factoring the remaining quadratic gets us the roots <imath>n = 3</imath> and <imath>n = 4.</imath> We can now express <imath>\frac{f(n)}{g(n)}</imath> as:
<cmath>\frac{(n + 1)(n - 4)(n - 2)}{(n + 1)(n - 4)(n - 3)}.</cmath> We can cancel the top and bottom to get:
<cmath>\frac{n - 2}{n - 3}.</cmath> 

Notice that the only values for which this expression is an integer are <imath>n = 4</imath> and <imath>n = 2</imath>, because they both cause the denominator to have a magnitude of <imath>1</imath>. However, <imath>n = 4</imath> is an extraneous solution as plugging it back into the original expression would make it evaluate to <imath>\frac{0}{0}</imath>. Our answer is then <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 2}</imath>.

~Milkdrinker and SixthGradeBookWorm927

==Solution 2==

We have <imath>\frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = \frac{n^3-5n^2+2n+8}{n^3-6n^2+5n+12} = 1 + \frac{n^2-3n-4}{n^3-6n^2+5n+12}.</imath> We factor the numerator as <imath>(n-4)(n+1)</imath>. Using synthetic division on the numerator's roots to factor the denominator, we find that the denominator is equivalent to <imath>(n+1)(n-3)(n-4)</imath>.

Simplifying, we get <imath>\frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = 1 + \frac{1}{n-3}</imath>. However, we ''must not'' include the values <imath>n=-1, 3,</imath> or <imath>4</imath>, or the original fraction will be undefined.

To have <imath>\frac{1}{n-3}</imath> be an integer, we require <imath>n-3 = 1</imath> or <imath>-1</imath>. This would give <imath>n = 2</imath> or <imath>4</imath>, but as in Solution 1, since <imath>n = 4</imath> must not be included, we deduce that there is only <imath>1</imath> possible value of <imath>n</imath>, namely <imath>n = 2</imath>. Hence the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 2}</imath>.

~OlympiadMaster

==Solution 3==

We have to plug in different values into <imath>\frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = \frac{n^3-5n^2+2n+8}{n^3-6n^2+5n+12} = 1 + \frac{n^2-3n-4}{n^3-6n^2+5n+12}.</imath> Because of the answer choices, we only really need to test <imath>n=1</imath>, <imath>n=2</imath>, <imath>n=3</imath>, <imath>n=4</imath>, and <imath>n=5</imath>. Plugging in each of these values leads to <imath>n=\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 2}</imath> as our answer, since <imath>n = 2</imath> is the only value that leads to an integer. Note that plugging in <imath>n = 4</imath> yields <imath>0/0</imath>, which is undefined.

~ AskNamanonyt
